subject: Cognitive Science
title: Falsifiability
description: A quick, practical guide to Falsifiability.

hook.text: "The universe is run by invisible elves." Can you disprove it? No. That's what makes it unscientific.

buildup.text: Karl Popper argued that a theory is scientific only if it could, in principle, be proven wrong.

discovery.text: Falsifiability is the line between science and non-science: testable claims can be wrong. And that's the point.

twist.text: Some fields game this: theories so flexible they explain anything cannot actually predict anything.

climax.text: Good mental models must be falsifiable too. If nothing could ever change your mind, it's not a model—it's faith.

punchline.text: If it can't be wrong, it can't be useful.

quiz.question: What does falsifiability require of a theory?
options: It must be possible to prove it wrong

details.summary: Karl Popper argued that a claim is scientific only if it can be proven wrong. Falsifiability is the line between science and pseudoscience. If no possible observation could disprove a theory, the theory explains everything and therefore explains nothing useful.
details.whyItMatters: Falsifiability teaches you to test your beliefs honestly. Claims that cannot be wrong are not informative, no matter how compelling they sound.
takeaways: A scientific claim must be disprovable by observation
Unfalsifiable claims explain everything and nothing
Seek evidence that could prove your beliefs wrong

faq.question: What is an example of an unfalsifiable claim?
faq.answer: The claim that invisible forces are secretly controlling events is unfalsifiable because any evidence against it can be reinterpreted as part of the conspiracy. There is no observation that could disprove it. Compare this to a specific, testable prediction that can actually fail.

faq.question: Is falsifiability the only criterion for good science?
faq.answer: No. Falsifiability is necessary but not sufficient. Good science also requires replicability, predictive power, internal consistency, and parsimony. Popper's criterion identifies what counts as scientific, but additional criteria distinguish good science from weak science.
